analysis.one_liner: Adds hearing aids and auditory rehabilitation to Medicare coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare currently excludes hearing aids and the services that go with them, so seniors pay out of pocket for devices that often cost thousands of dollars. This bill would have removed that exclusion and directed the Health and Human Services Secretary to set national coverage rules for hearing aids, modeled on what the Veterans Affairs and Defense departments already provide, and to cover auditory rehabilitation services. It was introduced in October 2009 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss, who would get hearing aids and rehabilitation services covered by Medicare instead of paying entirely out of pocket. Hearing health professionals and hearing aid makers would also gain a large new paying customer base.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare with hearing loss

how_it_helps.text: Strikes hearing aids and related examinations from Medicare's list of excluded items, opening the door to coverage [S3].

Directs the HHS Secretary to write national coverage rules for hearing aids based on benefits already offered by federal programs like the VA and Department of Defense, in consultation with hearing health professionals and trade organizations [S3].
Adds auditory rehabilitation and treatment services to the list of covered outpatient services and conforms Medicare's physician payment rules to include them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and, ultimately, taxpayers and beneficiaries through premiums, would bear the cost of covering hearing aids and related services, which typically run thousands of dollars per device.

drawbacks.text: Covering hearing aids would add new federal Medicare spending, which could put upward pressure on premiums and general revenue costs, since hearing aids are expensive devices that many beneficiaries would newly claim [S3].

The bill left the specifics — how much Medicare would pay and for which devices — to later coverage determinations modeled on VA and Defense benefits, so the actual benefit design and cost were undetermined at introduction [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted at a common problem: hearing loss affects a large share of seniors, and Medicare's exclusion forces them to pay retail prices for devices. The cost is added federal health spending, though Medicare would likely get wholesale rates and negotiated coverage rules rather than paying retail. The bill never advanced far enough for a serious cost estimate or a real debate on the tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on October 22, 2009, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Finance Committee the same day — its only action beyond introduction [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal spending stayed unchanged, and hearing aid makers and audiologists kept selling devices at private-market prices instead of Medicare reimbursement rates. Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss continued paying out of pocket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hearing aid sellers; beneficiaries kept paying out of pocket

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over Medicare legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the two-plus years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action during the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill drew no cosponsors, so its partisan support level was never tested.

industries.note: Medicare coverage would make hearing aids payable by a public program, creating a large new covered customer base. The bill directs coverage rules to be set in consultation with trade organizations, giving the industry a seat in shaping the benefit [S3].
The bill adds auditory rehabilitation and treatment services to covered Medicare benefits, creating billable services for hearing professionals [S3].
